sections.markdown:
## C — Impaired driving: alcohol, drugs, implied consent and drowsiness

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
Impairment is not limited to alcohol: drugs, including prescription and over the counter medicines, can seriously affect driving, and drowsy driving is also dangerous [A01].
Why it matters: Three sources of impairment.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
The drinking driver is the number one cause of fatal traffic crashes, and on average someone is killed by a drunk driver every forty minutes [A01].
Why it matters: Handbook statistic, stated as the handbook states it.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
It is against the law to drive under the influence of alcohol or other drugs, because drinking or drugged drivers lack good control of themselves and the vehicle and endanger their own lives and others [A01].
Why it matters: The basic prohibition.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
Vermont law treats a driver with a blood alcohol concentration of point zero eight or above as under the influence or impaired, but a person is impaired below that level too, and even one drink impairs judgment [A01].
Why it matters: Point zero eight is the legal line, not the safe line.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
A driver under twenty-one with an alcohol concentration of point zero two or more can receive a civil traffic violation, has the license suspended and must complete an alcohol and driving education program at personal expense [A01].
Why it matters: Point zero two is the under twenty-one threshold.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A02
Alcohol is a drug and a depressant that affects the thought process and does not give a lift, and the decisions made after drinking may well be faulty [A02].
Why it matters: Alcohol is a depressant, not a stimulant.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A02
Alcohol harms judgment so you no longer make good driving decisions or sense the risks you take, reduces overall vision, lets the mind wander so you cannot concentrate, and lowers comprehension so you may not realize what you are doing [A02].
Why it matters: Four of the six listed effects.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A02
Alcohol suppresses the senses so you do not feel speed and may speed without knowing it, and it lengthens reaction time so moving the foot from gas to brake takes longer, which can be the difference between arriving safely or not at all [A02].
Why it matters: The last two listed effects.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A02
Time is the only way to reduce the effects of alcohol, coffee, a cold shower or running around will not sober anyone up, and the body needs at least an hour per drink to process the alcohol, so several hours may pass before driving is safe [A02].
Why it matters: One hour per drink, minimum.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A02
Driving after taking other drugs or narcotics, even prescription or over the counter ones, can be as deadly as alcohol or deadlier for some people, since drugs can cause sleepiness and poor thinking, and time is again the only remedy [A02].
Why it matters: Legal drugs count.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A02
A conviction for driving under the influence or after taking drugs brings license suspension, a large fine, lawyer fees, payment for an alcohol education class, possible jail and higher insurance [A02].
Why it matters: Six consequences of a conviction.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A02
Vermont's implied consent law means that by getting a license a person agrees to take a test for alcohol or drugs when a police officer who suspects impairment asks, and refusing the test costs the license for at least six months [A02].
Why it matters: Refusal alone costs six months.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A02
Vermont has an administrative suspension process, so a license can be lost through a civil process before any criminal conviction for driving under the influence [A02].
Why it matters: Suspension can precede conviction.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A02
If you plan to drink, plan first: use a designated driver who agrees not to drink or use drugs and takes responsibility for getting everyone home, or call a parent or other responsible person for a safe ride [A02].
Why it matters: The designated driver must stay sober.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A03
Other safe plans are to stay overnight where you are if it is safe, to take friends seriously when they warn you not to drive, and to hand your keys before drinking to a non drinking friend who will not let you drive [A03].
Why it matters: Keys go to a sober friend in advance.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A03
Coffee, a shower or exercise cannot lower blood alcohol concentration or its effects; only time does, at a minimum of an hour per drink [A03].
Why it matters: Restated on this page: only time works.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A03
The Vermont Emergency Nurses Association sponsors signs at the sites of alcohol related fatal crashes, and each sign marks a place where someone died because of a drunk driver [A03].
Why it matters: The roadside signs have one meaning.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A03
A person worried about their drinking can contact the Vermont Helplink, a free and confidential alcohol and drug support and referral service run by the Department of Health [A03].
Why it matters: The named support service.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A03
Many crashes each year happen because a driver falls asleep at the wheel, often ending in a head on crash with another vehicle, a tree or a roadside object, and drowsy drivers can drive so poorly that they appear drunk [A03].
Why it matters: Drowsy driving mimics drunk driving.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A03
Signs of drowsy driving are trouble focusing or keeping the eyes open, repeated yawning, not remembering the last few miles, drifting out of the lane and missing traffic signs [A03].
Why it matters: Five warning signs.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A03
People most at risk of drowsy driving are those who drive without enough sleep, often young people, shift workers, people working very long hours and people who may not know they have a sleep disorder, and a driver who believes they can stay awake may fall asleep and crash instead [A03].
Why it matters: Four at risk groups.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A03
Avoid driving when drowsy, and if drowsiness strikes on the road find a safe place to pull over and stop, because opening the window or turning up the radio will not keep you awake and looking for ways to stay awake is itself the sign to stop and rest [A03].
Why it matters: Window and radio tricks fail.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

Misconceptions:
- Below point zero eight you are safe to drive: false, impairment begins below that level and even one drink affects judgment.
- Coffee or a cold shower speeds up sobering: false, only time works, at least an hour per drink.
- Refusing the breath test avoids all penalties: false, refusal costs the license for at least six months under implied consent.
- Prescription medicine cannot count as impaired driving: false, driving after prescription or over the counter drugs can be as deadly as alcohol and is treated the same.
- A loud radio and open window keep a drowsy driver safe: false, they do not keep you awake; pull over and rest.

Mnemonics:
- Eight for all, two for the young: the point zero eight and point zero two thresholds.
- An hour a drink, nothing less: the only way alcohol leaves the body.
- Refuse and lose six: refusing the implied consent test costs six months.

Glossary:
- Blood alcohol concentration: the measured share of alcohol in the blood, legally impaired at point zero eight and, under twenty-one, a violation at point zero two
- Implied consent: the agreement every licensed driver makes to take an alcohol or drug test when an officer who suspects impairment asks
- Administrative suspension: a civil process that can take a license away before a criminal conviction
- Designated driver: a person who agrees not to drink or use drugs and takes responsibility for driving the others home
- Depressant: a drug such as alcohol that slows the thought process rather than lifting it

Dynamic facts isolated:
- None: every rule in this section is stable handbook law for the pined edition; no officeholder, date or fee amount is carried as knowledge.
